Strzegowo Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Strzegowo, Poland

Not demolished. Strzegowo's first Jews settled around 1775, though significant population growth came only at the century's end alongside rapid industrialization; roughly 80 of 510 residents were Jewish by mid-19th century, reaching 591 (of 1,853) by 1921. Rabbi Jicchak Majer Piotrkowski, resident from 1904, led the community's independence at the start of the 20th century; about 600 Jews (30%+) lived there before WWII. At local Jewish request (to avoid Mława deportation), Germans established a Strzegowo ghetto in November 1941, absorbing over 1,000 Bieżun Jews that January and 200 more from Drobin and Sierpc that February. On September 2, 1942, Germans hanged 20 Jews on mutiny charges, burying them in Karwiński Forest; the ghetto's November 1942 liquidation sent residents directly to Treblinka or via Mława to Auschwitz-Birkenau. This cemetery, established at the end of the 19th century, received its last burial in 1941 before formal closure in 1964. In 1948, descendants exhumed and reburied 20 Jews murdered in 1942, erecting a Holocaust memorial later renovated in 1962 and again in 2002-2004 (initiated by Barbara Goldman with the Foundation for the Preservation of Jewish Heritage and the Polish-Jewish Program for the Restoration of Cemeteries), though it suffered further damage in 2004.
